# Tomato

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="tomato-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="tomato-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="tomato-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Fresh tomatoes are usually low in lead and cadmium: about 3% of monitoring results exceed the EU lead maximum of 50 µg/kg and about 4% the cadmium maximum of 20 µg/kg, and US market baskets were lower still.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Metals of concern:</strong>

Cadmium and lead first; mercury, nickel, chromium and arsenic rise at exposed growing sites.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/ahmed2023-trace-metals-tomato-wastewater|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ahmed A, Hassan I, Abd-Elrahman S, ElSayed M · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ahmed2023-trace-metals-tomato-wastewater">Trace metal concentrations in tomato fruits irrigated with industrial wastewater in Cairo and health risk assessment</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Science and Pollution Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ahmed2023-trace-metals-tomato-wastewater">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Growing site, irrigation water, nearby emitters and, after harvest, cookware.<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" </li>
<li>
<strong>Practical framing:</strong>

Ask where and how the tomatoes were grown, and for fresh-weight lead and cadmium results.<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shanshan Chen, Chunxia Yao, Jiaxin Zhou, Haiyao Ma, Jing Jin, Weiguo Song, Zhenpeng Kai · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables">Occurrence and Risk Assessment of Pesticides, Phthalates, and Heavy Metal Residues in Vegetables from Hydroponic and Conventional Cultivation</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Foods 13, 1151</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

## Tomato overview

<a id="hmi-ing-004"></a>
<a id="which-contamination-concerns-are-supported-for-this-ingredient-and-its-defined-forms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-005"></a>
<a id="which-sourcing-or-production-decisions-deserve-priority-on-the-available-evidence"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-006"></a>
<a id="which-evidence-gaps-most-limit-those-decisions"></a>

Fresh tomato usually carries little lead or cadmium. In 2,778 WHO GEMS/Food lead results for fresh tomato from 1998 to 2020, about two in three were below the laboratory’s detection limit, the median lay between 0 and 7.5 µg/kg, and 86 (3.1%) were above 50 µg/kg, the EU maximum for fruiting vegetables.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) results, with a median between 0 and 5 µg/kg, and 137 (4.3%) were above the EU maximum of 20 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants United States market baskets were lower still. In 27 FDA Total Diet Study samples of raw tomato bought from 2017 to 2020, cadmium was found in 24 at 1.0–7.6 µg/kg (median 3.3 µg/kg), while lead, total arsenic, mercury, nickel, chromium and uranium were below reporting limits of 1–50 µg/kg in every sample.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span The high values in the literature come from exposed growing sites, from studies reporting on a dry-weight basis, and from papers whose figures do not survive a check. Tomatoes grown near two Chinese coal-fired power plants held 9.8–76 µg/kg mercury against 0.73 µg/kg in a grocery-store sample, and Cairo tomatoes irrigated with industrial wastewater held about two and a half times the nickel and chromium of Nile-irrigated fruit.<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span <div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-tomato" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-tomato-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one subgroup and metal; a mean, median and range from the same samples are separate rows. Results on a fresh-weight basis, a dry-weight basis and an unstated basis are kept apart, because dried tomato is roughly ten to twenty times more concentrated than the fresh fruit. Ratings place a reported mean, median or sample result against a pooled HMI tomato reference on the same basis. Same-study contrasts compare a subgroup with its own study’s control, total or lowest subgroup. Experimental treatments, such as spiked irrigation water, are compared only with their own controls. Held rows failed a check against their own paper and are shown but not compared. Canned tomatoes, paste, sauce, ketchup and juice are separate foods with their own pages.</p>

class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" id="hmi-occurrence-tomato-methods" data-shared-occurrence-methods><summary>Shared dataset methods and interpretation</summary><div data-shared-evidence-content><p>Source summaries retain their original statistic, material, basis and censoring. Each source drawer identifies methods and overlapping samples. No matched reference or pooled distribution is inferred.</p></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:tomato-fresh-Pb:8fc27f3f9bc3"><summary>HMI tomato Pb reference, fresh weight · 3 sampling families</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:tomato-fresh-Pb:8fc27f3f9bc3"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI tomato Pb reference, fresh weight · 3 sampling families. Fresh tomato fruit, fresh (wet) weight, µg/kg. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>≤4</td><td>≤4</td><td>≤4</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>≤4</td><td>≤4</td><td>≤4</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>143 reference units; 3 sampling families. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>115</td><td>33%</td></tr><tr><td>FDA Total Diet Study</td><td>27</td><td>33%</td></tr><tr><td>Grochowska-Niedworok et al. 2020</td><td>1</td><td>33%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians from every compatible fresh weight fresh-tomato sampling family in the evidence ledger: WHO GEMS/Food medians by reporting region, year, growing-system label and origin label (random sampling only), FDA Total Diet Study market-basket samples, per-sample results printed by surveys, single-composite means and published subgroup medians. Each family has equal total weight; subgroups have equal weight within a family. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima of several samples never enter as observations. Experimental treatments, wastewater or effluent irrigation and mining or power-plant exposure sites never enter.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1–Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>An evidence-library reference for fresh tomato on a fresh weight basis, not a probability sample of any market. GEMS/Food regions are reporting regions, not growing origins. Fresh-weight and dry-weight results are never converted into one another, because few sources report the moisture of the tomatoes they measured. The paper reports no LOD, blank, CRM or recovery for flame AAS Pb, so the values cannot be checked against the paper&#39;s own QA; the authors themselves note Pb is &#39;much higher&#39; than published values from Egypt, China and Saudi Arabia (Figs 1a–1c). Extracted as printed; treat with caution. Table 1 prints tomato &#39;Hymidity (%)&#39; 91.10. The authors&#39; EDI formula uses C in &#39;µg/kg fresh weight&#39;; Table 3 tomato EDI values reproduce exactly when the dry-weight value is multiplied by (1 − 0.911) and by an ingestion rate of 36.62 g/day and divided by 69.6 kg, so the authors&#39; implied fresh-weight concentration is ≈2.40 mg/kg fw. This fresh-weight figure is derived, not printed; finding kept on the printed dry-weight basis. Single composite per food item (~4 kg from different sellers), two 3 g mixed sub-samples analysed, arithmetic mean reported; no SD. Authors list tomatoes among the items with the highest Pb (with onions, carrots, potatoes) and attribute high Pb to wastewater irrigation and leaded petrol traffic emissions (speculative, not tested). n = 1 composite food-item sample (two analytical sub-samples).</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Shared samples and study overlap</p><p>Subgroup rows, statistics of the same subgroup and the study total share samples; they are not independent results.</p><p>Each table row describes a food/analyte result. The text also calls the samples &#39;fresh fruit and vegetables&#39; while stating &#39;concentrations determined were based on sample dry weight&#39;. The conclusion is only reconcilable if the limit is compared on a fresh-weight basis (0.511 x (1-0.940) ≈ 0.031 mg/kg), which the paper never states. Basis per text p. 3: &#39;The heavy metal concentrations determined were based on sample dry weight.&#39; Table 2 prints tomato moisture 94.0%; a fresh-weight equivalent would be ≈0.031 mg/kg but the source does not make this conversion (not applied). &#39;±&#39; not defined (SD or SE); three replicate analyses per food item from a composite. Method: hmi-pooled-reference-v2.</p><p>No admitted reference</p><p>The reference is computed by HMI from admitted evidence, not copied from a study baseline. Different HMI scopes are not one common ranking.</p></details></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Collection period</p><p data-timeline-scope>2022</p><div data-selected-timeline><p>No year-by-year sample register is reconstructed from this summary.</p></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Geographic scope</p><p data-regional-scope>Tomato</p><div data-selected-regional><p>Reported growing area.</p></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Sampling, analysis and reporting limits</p><p>wet digestion of 0.5 g dried powder with 9 ml HNO3/HCl/H2SO4 on hot plate, filtered, made up with de-ionised water; flame AAS (Perkin Elmer 2130).</p><p>no non-detects reported; no LOD given</p><p>The concentration formula uses a 20 ml volume while the digest was made up to 100 ml, so every value may be five times too low; the paper does not resolve which volume applies. Different HMI scopes are not one common ranking.</p></details></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Collection period</p><p data-timeline-scope>Collection date unreported</p><div data-selected-timeline><p>No year-by-year sample register is reconstructed from this summary.</p></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Geographic scope</p><p data-regional-scope>Tomato</p><div data-selected-regional><p>Reported growing area.</p></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Sampling, analysis and reporting limits</p><p>NaI(Tl) gamma spectrometry, 36,000 s counting; 238U via 214Bi 1.76 MeV line after ~4 weeks sealing for secular equilibrium.</p><p>no censoring for tomato (detected); BDL used for other crops without a numeric detection limit</p><p>Checked against the paper: Unit is activity (Bq/kg), not mass concentration, and the uncertainty is a counting uncertainty rather than a between-sample SD; not directly comparable with ICP-MS uranium in µg/kg. 238U was quantified indirectly from the 1.76 MeV gamma line of 214Bi (Section 2.2), so the value reflects radium-series daughters assuming secular equilibrium, not chemically measured uranium. &#39;±&#39; values are combined counting uncertainties, not sample SD (p.35). Mining-impacted soils: farm soil 238U 10.9-470.6 Bq/kg dw (Table 2). The text calls the 238U unit &#39;Bq kg1&#39; (minus sign lost in extraction).</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Shared samples and study overlap</p><p>Subgroup rows, statistics of the same subgroup and the study total share samples; they are not independent results.</p><p>Each table row describes a food/analyte result. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach tomatoes

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

Most of what reaches tomato fruit reflects the growing site: soil, irrigation water and air. In a four-year Chinese field trial, fruit irrigated with half reclaimed water held more cadmium (29 against 18 µg/kg) and chromium (61 against 49 µg/kg) than fruit irrigated with groundwater, although only the chromium difference approached statistical significance.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2015-reclaimed-water-through-field-trials-on-the-content|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2015-reclaimed-water-through-field-trials-on-the-content">reclaimed water through field trials on the content and distribution of heavy metals in both tomatoes</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2015-reclaimed-water-through-field-trials-on-the-content">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Cairo, fruit from farms irrigated with untreated industrial wastewater held 760 µg/kg chromium and 1,630 µg/kg nickel against 290 and 610 µg/kg on farms irrigated from the Nile; the same paper’s lead and cadmium values cannot be reconciled with its own soil data and are held.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ahmed2023-trace-metals-tomato-wastewater|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ahmed A, Hassan I, Abd-Elrahman S, ElSayed M · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ahmed2023-trace-metals-tomato-wastewater">Trace metal concentrations in tomato fruits irrigated with industrial wastewater in Cairo and health risk assessment</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Science and Pollution Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ahmed2023-trace-metals-tomato-wastewater">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Air is the main route for mercury near large emitters. Around a Chinese coal-fired power plant, tomato mercury fell from 76.3 µg/kg at the nearest site to 9.8 µg/kg at the farthest, and two sites near a second plant held 71.8 and 29.8 µg/kg, against 0.73 µg/kg in tomatoes from a grocery store.<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Experiments show the same dependence on water and soil. Fruit arsenic rose to 0.18 and 0.43 µg/g dry weight when irrigation water was spiked to 500 and 1,000 µg/L arsenic in Burkina Faso, about 0.02 and 0.05 µg/g on a fresh-weight basis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina|26]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Clair-Caliot G, Marks SJ, Hug SJ, Bretzler A, N&#39;guessan ND, Tihe SFK, Lalanne F · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Uptake of Arsenic by Irrigated Vegetables and Cooked Food Products in Burkina Faso</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Water</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Egypt, fruit grown with agricultural drainage water held 1,000 µg/kg nickel in a greenhouse plot and 88 µg/kg in a field plot, and remediating the soil with clay minerals and treating the water lowered these to 250 and 18 µg/kg; cadmium was not detected in any treatment.<sup class="cite">[[sources/salem2024-tomato-remediated-soil-egypt|27]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Salem SH, Saber M, Gadow S, Kabary H, Zaghloul A · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/salem2024-tomato-remediated-soil-egypt">Influence of the use of remediated soil and agricultural drainage water on the safety of tomato fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Science and Pollution Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/salem2024-tomato-remediated-soil-egypt">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In a Dominican greenhouse trial, lead, cadmium and arsenic stayed below 10 µg/kg in fruit whether the plants received mineral fertiliser, a seaweed-based biofertiliser or nothing.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rodriguez-rodriguez2026-sargassum-biofertilizer-tomato-trace-elements|28]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rodríguez-Rodríguez R, Sánchez-García A, Ruiz-Lozano JM, Aroca R · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rodriguez-rodriguez2026-sargassum-biofertilizer-tomato-trace-elements">Trace Element Content in Tomato Fruit Grown with Sargassum-Based Biofertilizer</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Agronomy</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rodriguez-rodriguez2026-sargassum-biofertilizer-tomato-trace-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>



<a id="ranges-by-source-region-and-variety"></a>
## Which tomatoes and growing conditions measured lower

<a id="hmi-ing-013"></a>
<a id="how-do-concentrations-vary-by-origin-growing-conditions-variety-and-harvest-period"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-014"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-distinguishes-within-lot-between-lot-supplier-and-production-system-variation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-015"></a>
<a id="which-comparisons-support-a-sourcing-decision-and-where-would-geographic-or-supplier-generalization-be-unjustified"></a>

For lead, the lowest results came from the United States and from Americas monitoring submissions. All 27 FDA market-basket samples were below 4 µg/kg, and in GEMS/Food the detected lead results had a median of 2.1 µg/kg in the Americas, 4.3 µg/kg in the Western Pacific and 18 µg/kg in Europe, with 2.2%, 2.6% and 3.7% of results above 50 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Part of that difference is analytical: European lead results had a median detection limit of 8 µg/kg, often 10–50 µg/kg, against 1 µg/kg in the Americas, so this is a tentative pattern among reporting regions, not a sourcing preference for a country.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Growing-system labels did not separate lead in the monitoring data, but one controlled comparison did. In Americas submissions from 2014 to 2016, greenhouse-labelled tomatoes had a detected lead median of 2.2 µg/kg (54 of 156 detected), organic-labelled 1.7 µg/kg (19 of 46) and unlabelled 2.0 µg/kg; only three of ten field-labelled results were detected, too few to compare.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Shanghai, hydroponically grown tomatoes held 5.6 µg/kg lead and cadmium combined against 47.9 µg/kg for soil-grown tomatoes from 20 and 22 farm samples, a significant difference; the paper does not give the two metals separately for tomato or state the weight basis.<sup class="cite">[[sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shanshan Chen, Chunxia Yao, Jiaxin Zhou, Haiyao Ma, Jing Jin, Weiguo Song, Zhenpeng Kai · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables">Occurrence and Risk Assessment of Pesticides, Phthalates, and Heavy Metal Residues in Vegetables from Hydroponic and Conventional Cultivation</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Foods 13, 1151</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Type also mattered in one Romanian survey. After washing in tap water, red cherry tomatoes from the market held 18.6 µg/kg lead and no detectable cadmium against 66.8 µg/kg lead and 16.5 µg/kg cadmium in standard tomatoes, while yellow cherry tomatoes held 51.3 µg/kg lead and 23.5 µg/kg cadmium.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bora FD, Bunea A, Pop SR, Banita SI, Dusa DS, Chira A, Bunea CI · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Quantification and Reduction in Heavy Metal Residues in Some Fruits and Vegetables: A Case Study Galați County, Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Horticulturae</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Total arsenic did not follow: it was 334 µg/kg in red cherry and 389 µg/kg in standard tomatoes, so the type lowest in lead was not lowest in arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bora FD, Bunea A, Pop SR, Banita SI, Dusa DS, Chira A, Bunea CI · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Quantification and Reduction in Heavy Metal Residues in Some Fruits and Vegetables: A Case Study Galați County, Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Horticulturae</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

For cadmium, fresh-weight means were lowest in Poland and western Iran and highest in Egypt and northern Iran. Ten Polish tomatoes averaged 3 µg/kg and 50 composites from Hamadan 3 µg/kg, against 9–15 µg/kg in Tehran, 25.5 µg/kg in Ismailia and 27 µg/kg in Babol; the GEMS/Food detected medians were 5 µg/kg in Europe and 9–12 µg/kg in the Americas, Western Pacific and Eastern Mediterranean.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="are-greenhouse-or-organic-tomatoes-lower-in-lead" data-anchor="are-greenhouse-or-organic-tomatoes-lower-in-lead" data-question="Are greenhouse or organic tomatoes lower in lead?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Are greenhouse or organic tomatoes lower in lead?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Not clearly in the monitoring data: Americas submissions labelled greenhouse or organic had detected lead medians of 2.2 and 1.7 µg/kg against 2.0 µg/kg for unlabelled tomatoes.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The one controlled comparison of growing systems found hydroponic tomatoes far lower in lead and cadmium combined than soil-grown tomatoes, 5.6 against 47.9 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shanshan Chen, Chunxia Yao, Jiaxin Zhou, Haiyao Ma, Jing Jin, Weiguo Song, Zhenpeng Kai · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables">Occurrence and Risk Assessment of Pesticides, Phthalates, and Heavy Metal Residues in Vegetables from Hydroponic and Conventional Cultivation</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Foods 13, 1151</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/chen2024-shanghai-hydroponic-vegetables">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-places-measured-the-lowest-cadmium-in-fresh-tomatoes" data-anchor="which-places-measured-the-lowest-cadmium-in-fresh-tomatoes" data-question="Which places measured the lowest cadmium in fresh tomatoes?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which places measured the lowest cadmium in fresh tomatoes?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

On a fresh-weight basis, the lowest means were 3 µg/kg in Poland and in Hamadan, Iran, and the FDA median was 3.3 µg/kg; Tehran, Ismailia and Babol were higher at 9–27 µg/kg.<sup <a id="processing-effects"></a>
<a id="processing-effects-and-derivatives"></a>
## Washing, cooking and processed products

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

Washing removes part of the metal measured on tomatoes, and an acidic soak removed more. In Romania, soaking tap-washed market tomatoes in 5% vinegar lowered total arsenic from 389 to 202 µg/kg, cadmium from 16.5 to 12.2 µg/kg and lead from 66.8 to 54.0 µg/kg on a fresh-weight basis; a 10% soak gave similar results.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bora FD, Bunea A, Pop SR, Banita SI, Dusa DS, Chira A, Bunea CI · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Quantification and Reduction in Heavy Metal Residues in Some Fruits and Vegetables: A Case Study Galați County, Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Horticulturae</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The paper’s text reports larger reductions than its own tables, and there was no unwashed comparison, so the measured effect is the tables’ smaller one.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bora FD, Bunea A, Pop SR, Banita SI, Dusa DS, Chira A, Bunea CI · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Quantification and Reduction in Heavy Metal Residues in Some Fruits and Vegetables: A Case Study Galați County, Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Horticulturae</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Cooking cannot destroy a metal, and cookware can add one. Boiling Burkina Faso tomatoes in arsenic-free water did not lower arsenic per gram of dry matter in fruit from spiked irrigation: it was 0.43 µg/g before and 0.71 µg/g after.<sup class="cite">[[sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina|26]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Clair-Caliot G, Marks SJ, Hug SJ, Bretzler A, N&#39;guessan ND, Tihe SFK, Lalanne F · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Uptake of Arsenic by Irrigated Vegetables and Cooked Food Products in Burkina Faso</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Water</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Baking fresh tomato in aluminium foil raised aluminium from 80 to as much as 370 µg/kg fresh weight, and simmering commercial tomato sauce with stainless steel for six hours raised nickel from about 0.15 to about 5–6 mg/kg, an effect that fell to about 0.7 mg/kg once the steel had been used for six cooking cycles.<sup class="cite">[[sources/hobbie2014-stainless-steel-ni-cr-leaching|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Hobbie KA, Kamerud KL, Anderson KA · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/hobbie2014-stainless-steel-ni-cr-leaching">Stainless Steel Leaches Nickel and Chromium into Foods During Cooking</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Society of Toxicology 2014 Annual Meeting (poster)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/hobbie2014-stainless-steel-ni-cr-leaching">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/dordevic2019-aluminum-foil-culinary-baking-czech|32]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dordevic D, Buchtova H, Jancikova S, Macharackova B, Jarosova M, Vitez T, Kushkevych I · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dordevic2019-aluminum-foil-culinary-baking-czech">Aluminum contamination of food during culinary preparation: Case study with aluminum foil and consumers&#39; preferences</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Science &amp; Nutrition</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dordevic2019-aluminum-foil-culinary-baking-czech">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Canned and concentrated products are separate foods. Studies of canned tomato products measured tin migrating from the can during storage, which fresh tomato does not carry; those results are on the canned tomato and tomato paste pages.<sup class="cite">[[sources/buculei2012-tin-iron-migration-canned-food-romania|33]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Buculei A, Gutt G, Amariei S, Dabija A, Constantinescu G · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/buculei2012-tin-iron-migration-canned-food-romania">Study regarding the tin and iron migration from metallic cans into foodstuff during storage</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Agroalimentary Processes and Technologies, 18(4), 299-303</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/buculei2012-tin-iron-migration-canned-food-romania">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/trandafir2012-tin-canned-foods-icp-ms|34]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Trandafir I, Nour V, Ionica ME · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/trandafir2012-tin-canned-foods-icp-ms">Determination of Tin in Canned Foods by Inductively Coupled Plasma-Mass Spectrometry</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Polish Journal of Environmental Studies</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/trandafir2012-tin-canned-foods-icp-ms">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

No single lever lowered every metal. In Seville urban gardens, the peri-urban plot had the lowest chromium and nickel but the highest cadmium and, narrowly, lead, and among Romanian tomatoes the cherry type lowest in lead was not lowest in arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bora FD, Bunea A, Pop SR, Banita SI, Dusa DS, Chira A, Bunea CI · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Quantification and Reduction in Heavy Metal Residues in Some Fruits and Vegetables: A Case Study Galați County, Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Horticulturae</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/rossini-oliva2024-urban-garden-vegetables-spain|24]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rossini-Oliva S, López Nuñez R · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rossini-oliva2024-urban-garden-vegetables-spain">Is it healthy urban agriculture? Some post-harvest controls have their own costs. A vinegar soak also changes the fruit, and the Romanian study did not measure quality; stainless steel’s nickel and chromium release fell with repeated use, so a new pan matters more than an old one; Ask where and how the tomatoes were grown, not only where they were packed. ## Exposure from tomato

<a id="hmi-ing-031"></a>

Tomato is eaten in large amounts, so even low concentrations matter for intake. Adults ate 109 g of tomato a day in an Iranian survey and 75.6 g of fresh tomato a day in Lebanon, the second-highest intake of any food in that survey.<sup class="cite">[[sources/heshmati2020-iran-vegetables-cereals-pb-cd|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ali Heshmati, Fereshteh Mehri, Javad class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/heshmati2020-iran-vegetables-cereals-pb-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/el-daouk2020-aluminum-food-lebanon|38]]<span Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/el-daouk2020-aluminum-food-lebanon">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Hamadan, tomato gave an estimated 0.011 µg/kg body weight a day of lead and 0.005 µg/kg of cadmium, and in Ismailia it supplied 16% of estimated cadmium intake and 9% of lead intake.<sup class="cite">[[sources/heshmati2020-iran-vegetables-cereals-pb-cd|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ali Heshmati, Fereshteh Mehri, Javad Karami-Momtaz, Amin Mousavi Khaneghah · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" National diet studies put tomato among the minor sources. Australia’s 25th Total Diet Study found that tomatoes, eggplant and okra together supplied 2–3% of cadmium exposure, and no source in the ledger estimated tomato’s share of arsenic or mercury intake.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fsanz2019-25th-australian-total-diet-study|39]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Food Standards Australia New Zealand · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fsanz2019-25th-australian-total-diet-study">25th Australian Total Diet Study</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Standards Australia New Zealand</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fsanz2019-25th-australian-total-diet-study">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

## Tomato FAQs

<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Cadmium is the metal most often detected in fresh tomato, usually at a few µg/kg: half of 3,197 GEMS/Food results and 24 of 27 FDA samples had measurable cadmium.<sup
